title: Remittance subscription backlog
telemetry: Protected synthetic fixture serving Cloud Run service and revision descriptions, Cloud Logging entries for the subscriber service (cloud_run_revision) and the subscription (pubsub_subscription), and an owner-run export of Cloud Monitoring subscription samples written to Cloud Logging. The subscription is global; us-east4 identifies its subscriber deployment. Each read returns a compiled packet, not a native API response
owner: Priya, Remittance on-call, owns the investigation. The remit-applier application owner owns subscriber code, release and capacity decisions; the remittance gateway owner publishes remit-instructions and owns the message schema; the ledger owner reconciles applied remittances; the Observability platform team owns Logging sinks and the metric exporter. ITO coordinates the existing TLC and change approvals
task: Priya has asked you to investigate the growing backlog on remit-apply-sub in synthetic-remittance-prod. Using the listed reads, determine what the evidence supports about the mechanism of the delay for 2026-10-14 12:50-13:18 UTC, and return a bounded technical finding with the supporting evidence, remaining unknowns and the next useful check with its owner. The existing TLC is the coordination channel. No change is approved.
common_evidence:
[UNTRUSTED] Synthetic supplied observations, not live cloud measurements. All times are UTC on 2026-10-14.
Packet released at 13:18:00Z; the latest Cloud Monitoring sample in it is 13:15:00Z.
Project synthetic-remittance-prod; pull subscription remit-apply-sub on topic remit-instructions; the subscription and topic are global resources.
Subscriber: Cloud Run service remit-applier in us-east4 pulls remit-apply-sub; it receives no HTTP work.
Subscription configuration snapshot (13:16:00Z): pull delivery; acknowledgment deadline 60 s; retry policy exponential backoff, minimum 10 s, maximum 600 s; no dead-letter topic; no filter; message ordering off; exactly-once delivery off.
Subscriber service card (application owner): each instance runs 4 handler threads, each handling one message at a time; client flow control leases up to 200 messages per instance and extends leases while they wait; a message is acked after its ledger write succeeds and nacked when the handler raises.
Subscriber logging (service card): ERROR for ledger-write failures and shutdown; WARNING for payload rejections; one INFO event=delivery record for every delivery of a message whose ID falls in hash bucket 0 of 20 (about 1 in 20 message IDs; every delivery of a sampled ID is logged).
13:10:30Z alert opened: remit-apply-sub num_undelivered_messages above 2,500 for 2 minutes.
Cloud Monitoring num_undelivered_messages: 12:50:00Z 40; 12:55:00Z 40; 13:00:00Z 1,040; 13:05:00Z 2,040; 13:10:00Z 3,040; 13:15:00Z 4,040. The same hour on 2026-10-13 stayed below 60.
13:00-13:15Z publisher summary: 6,000 unique remittance instructions accepted, about 400 per minute and steady since 12:30Z; no publish errors.
13:00-13:15Z ledger-owner dashboard: about 3,000 unique remittances applied, about 200 per minute; the same hour on 2026-10-13 applied about 400 per minute.
Change calendar: remit-applier release 5.8.0 (revision remit-applier-00031-kef) took 100% of the service at 12:53:10Z, replacing 5.7.4 (remit-applier-00030-dux); no publisher, subscription or ledger change is listed for 2026-10-14.
Applied remittances are effects. This fixture models ordinary at-least-once delivery; no effect deduplication guarantee is supplied.
No seek, replay, acknowledgment, subscription edit, scaling change, rollback or ledger write is approved.
competing_lead: Identical, attractive reads point each variant toward the wrong mechanism. Toward poison messages (wrong in A): subscriber-errors shows recurring 'message nacked for redelivery' ledger-409 entries, one message ID nacked twice at 13:02, and nacks on SIGTERM at the 12:53 release, while subscriber-revision shows release 5.8.0 accepting only schema version 6. Toward insufficient capacity (wrong in B): subscriber-service shows the subscriber fixed at two instances, the change calendar puts release 5.8.0 about two minutes before applied throughput halved, and backlog and oldest age rising together match Pub/Sub's documented 'subscribers not keeping up' pattern. Only subscriber-deliveries (handler time against eight threads; repeated message IDs) and subscription-metrics (oldest-age slope of 0.5 versus 1.0 s/s) separate the mechanisms; in C both return no usable observation, so neither mechanism is supported.

Cloud Logging, resource cloud_run_revision, service remit-applier, jsonPayload.event=delivery.
0 entries matched within gcloud's default one-day freshness window.
Logging configuration note captured by the Observability platform team at 13:17:00Z: the project's _Default sink has had exclusion filter drop-delivery-events (jsonPayload.event="delivery") since 2026-10-12T16:20:00Z under CHG-45877, and no other sink in synthetic-remittance-prod routes these entries. Subscriber delivery records for this window were not stored.

a.conclusion: Subscriber processing capacity is below the arrival rate. Every sampled delivery takes about 2.3-2.5 s, and eight handler threads (two fixed instances with four threads each) at about 2.4 s complete about 8 / 2.4 x 60 = 200 messages per minute, matching the ~200 applied per minute against ~400 arriving; the ~200-per-minute shortfall equals the backlog growth of 1,000 per 5 minutes. The sample agrees: 49 acked deliveries in about 296 s at 1 in 20 IDs is about 199 per minute, so the threads are saturated. Oldest unacked age rises 150 s per 300 s (0.5 s/s), less than elapsed time, so the oldest messages keep being acknowledged and no message has stayed unacknowledged since the 12:55 onset. The ERROR-log nacks are ledger 409 conflicts at about 0.4 per minute both before and after 12:55, and the one sampled conflict (16429770318845207) was acked on redelivery 13.7 s later; they cannot account for a 200-per-minute shortfall. Why the handler now takes about 2.4 s, when the same hour yesterday applied ~400 per minute, is not established; release 5.8.0 and ledger latency are candidates, not demonstrated causes.
next_checks: The remit-applier application owner breaks down handler time (ledger call versus local processing) for 5.8.0 against 5.7.4 and the previous day before proposing any thread, instance or rollback change through ITO.
The ledger owner checks ledger write latency and conflict rates since 12:50 UTC and confirms whether more concurrent writers are safe before any capacity increase.

Priya tracks applied rate, backlog and oldest unacked age over later complete intervals; recovery requires the applied rate to exceed arrivals and the age to fall, not one good sample. The ledger owner reconciles applied remittance IDs before any separate replay or disposition decision.
unsupported: Diagnosing poison or unsupported messages from the ERROR-log nacks, the repeated conflict at 13:02 or ACCEPTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS=6, which the delivery sample and the age slope contradict.
Naming release 5.8.0 or the ledger as the demonstrated cause, or promising that a specific instance or thread count or a rollback will clear the backlog.
Seeking, replaying, acknowledging or discarding messages to clear the backlog.
unknowns: Why handler time is about 2.4 s and whether release 5.8.0 or the ledger contributes.
Whether the ledger can absorb more concurrent writes, and whether the 1-in-20 delivery sample represents all messages.
Effects of messages delivered more than once, which at-least-once delivery permits.

b.conclusion: A subset of messages fails on every delivery and is redelivered while others succeed. In the delivery sample, six message IDs are each nacked twice, 10-22 s apart, in 4-9 ms, and none of the 38 nacked IDs is ever acked, while six other IDs ack once in 459-513 ms. Oldest unacked age rises 300 s per 300 s (1.0 s/s), so the oldest message has not been acknowledged since about 12:55. At about 0.49 s per successful message and ~200 applied per minute, the eight handler threads spend about 98 of 480 thread-seconds per minute on successes; about 1,650 nacked deliveries per minute (44 in 32 s at 1 in 20 IDs) at about 6 ms add about 10, so the threads are about a fifth to a quarter busy (a quarter if the page's own ack rate of about 226 per minute is used) and a shortage of threads or instances does not explain the shortfall, despite the fixed two instances and backlog and age rising together. With capacity idle, the ~200 per minute of ~400 arriving that are not applied are the messages failing on every delivery, matching the backlog growth. Why they fail is not in these reads; ACCEPTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS=6, release 5.8.0 and an unlisted publisher change are hypotheses, not demonstrated causes.
next_checks: The remit-applier application owner reads the WARNING payload-rejection records for the repeatedly nacked IDs (for example 16429773141226833 and 16429779749983738) and compares the payloads 5.8.0 accepts with 5.7.4, without consuming or acknowledging more messages.
The remittance gateway owner checks with sanitized metadata whether published payloads (schema version or fields) changed since about 12:55 UTC.

The ledger owner reconciles applied remittance IDs before the owners choose, through ITO, a compatibility fix, rollback or approved disposition for the failing messages; Priya then watches applied rate, repeated-ID nacks, oldest age and backlog.
unsupported: Diagnosing insufficient subscriber capacity from the fixed two instances, the release timing or backlog and age rising together, and scaling as the fix.
Naming the failure's cause (a schema version, release 5.8.0 or the publisher) as established from these reads.
Treating a nack as proof of no effect for every message, or using nacks, acknowledgment, seek, discard or an unapproved dead-letter topic to clear the backlog.
unknowns: Why the failing messages fail, and when the first was published (the age series points to about 12:55).
Whether release 5.8.0, a publisher change or both introduced the failure.
The full set of affected messages and whether any already produced effects.

c.conclusion: The evidence does not establish a mechanism. The backlog grows 1,000 per 5 minutes because about 200 of about 400 arriving messages per minute are applied, which fits both subscriber capacity below the arrival rate and a subset of messages failing on every delivery. The two observations that would separate them are missing: delivery records are excluded from storage by a _Default sink exclusion since 2026-10-12, and the metric export no longer carries oldest unacked age. The fixed two instances, release 5.8.0, ACCEPTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS=6 and the background ledger-409 nacks fit either story or neither. A supported answer holds the conclusion open, names the missing observations and their owners, and recommends no fix.
next_checks: Priya or the Observability platform team reads subscription/oldest_unacked_message_age for remit-apply-sub from Cloud Monitoring for 12:50-13:15 UTC: a rise of about 1 s per second points to messages that never complete, about 0.5 s per second to a drain at half the arrival rate.

The remit-applier application owner supplies per-delivery outcomes by message ID and handler time for the window from its own records; restoring delivery records in Logging is a separately approved change by the Observability platform team.
The ledger owner reconciles applied remittance IDs; no scaling, rollback, replay, seek or acknowledgment until a mechanism is established and its owner approves a change through ITO.
unsupported: Concluding insufficient capacity from the fixed two instances or from the arrival and applied rates alone.
Concluding poison messages from the ERROR-log nacks, release 5.8.0 or ACCEPTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS=6.
Treating zero delivery records as zero failed deliveries.
Recommending scaling, rollback, replay, seek, discard or acknowledgment as a fix.
unknowns: The oldest unacked age trend, handler time and thread utilization, and whether any message IDs repeat without acknowledgment.
Why applied throughput halved relative to the previous day and what release 5.8.0 changed.

sources.claim: A negative acknowledgment or an expired acknowledgment deadline triggers per-message exponential backoff while other messages keep flowing; delays range from 0 to 600 seconds, with defaults of 10 seconds minimum and 600 seconds maximum. Google does not document the exact backoff schedule, so the fixture's redelivery spacing is illustrative and ungraded.

oldest_unacked_message_age is the age of the oldest unacknowledged message in the backlog; when it rises together with num_undelivered_messages, subscribers are not keeping up; repeated nacks lead to duplicates and high delivery delay, and nacks should not be used to skip messages. Variant B relies on the first pattern being a plausible but wrong reading.

A small, steady backlog with a steadily growing oldest age suggests a few messages that cannot be processed; Google recommends the by_region backlog metrics and warns of gaps of up to several minutes. The fixture uses the global metric names for a single-deployment subscriber and states its own sample times.

subscription/num_undelivered_messages counts unacknowledged (backlog) messages and subscription/oldest_unacked_message_age is the oldest unacknowledged message's age in seconds; both are sampled every 60 seconds and may not be visible for up to 120 seconds, so the 13:15 sample is available to a 13:17 export.

Pub/Sub offers at-least-once delivery with no ordering guarantee unless ordering keys are used, and repeatedly attempts delivery of unacknowledged messages. The 0.5 versus 1.0 s/s age slopes assume roughly oldest-first draining in A and are corroborating, not exact; B is decided with the repeated-ID delivery evidence.

The delivery-attempt count is populated when a dead-letter topic is enabled; without one the field is not set. The fixture has no dead-letter topic, so redelivery must be inferred by counting message IDs.

A sink does not route a log entry that matches one of its exclusion filters, exclusions apply as entries are received, and sinks cannot route entries retroactively; variant C states that no other sink stores the excluded delivery records.
gcloud logging read defaults to a one-day freshness window and newest-first order, and --limit caps the entries returned; the packets reorder entries oldest first and say so.

Cloud Run sends SIGTERM 10 seconds before shutting down an instance, and instance-based billing allocates CPU for the instance lifetime, which a pull subscriber on a service needs. When the old revision's instances stopped after traffic moved is not documented and is ungraded.
cloud_run_revision has project_id, service_name, revision_name, location and configuration_name labels; pubsub_subscription has project_id and subscription_id labels.
UpdateSubscription is recorded as an Admin Activity audit log; the fixture's empty audit read shows only that no matching entry fell inside the one-day freshness window.
